Copper Quarterly October 2010 # Executive Preview ## Copper flying to a new all-time high - This note updates CRU’s analysis of the copper market outlook in advance of LME Week. We will issue our final forecast later in October, taking on board any new developments and issues that may come to light during our conversations and discussions with clients and industry participants over LME week. - **Consumption is strong and growth is still centred on Asia** , with good performance from all products (especially electrical and electronics). **Despite few disruptions, supply growth is subdued this year** . We now forecast a small refined market deficit for 2010. - Consumption growth is expected to moderate next year as restocking ends and substitution losses increase in response to high and volatile prices. On the supply side, we expect to see only modest growth due to mine plan revisions, project delays and scrap shortages. Therefore, we believe **the market will move into a considerable deficit in 2011** . - In addition, fears of an imminent double dip recession are all but gone, thus boosting sentiment about demand prospects and prompting **fresh investment inflows into copper** . - The refined copper deficits in 2010 and 2011 and consequent draw down in stocks will push stocks-to-consumption ratios down to the lows seen in 2004 and 2005. As a result, **we now forecast prices rising to new highs in 2011, triggering a further round of significant and permanent demand destruction, focussed on brass mills** . #### **Strong price recovery with high side bias** LME cash price and supply/demand balance, annual 2000-2015

CRU International Limited confidential Copper Quarterly October 2010 Executive Preview 3 #### Consumption strong but facing demand destruction threat Consumption is strong, with the Asia-centric recovery from 2009 well underway. Growth in consumption in North America and Western Europe is lagging the world average, but there are no longer fears of an imminent double dip recession. Higher and volatile prices in 2011 will lead to the onset of a round of significant and permanent demand destruction (rationing in mainly non-electrical applications). Scrap is already being rationed. Given that the market is tightening sooner than previously expected, the cumulative effect of slower growth means our consumption forecast for 2013 is 500,000t lower than in the July Quarterly. CRU International Limited confidential 4 Copper Quarterly October 2010 Executive Preview #### Mine supply lagging Mine output growth is the main constraint on the market. In 2010, mine supply has been r

emarkably free of disruptions, but is on course to fall slightly. Mine plan revisions (especially at Grasberg and Escondida) and lower guidance from producers across most regions will constrain total mine output in 2011, which is forecast to be about 400,000t lower than in our July Quarterly. As production from projects and new mines comes through, annual mine supply growth will rise to a peak of 6.2% in 2013, and exceed the level of output we presented three months ago by 2014. CRU International Limited confidential Copper Quarterly October 2010 Executive Preview 5 #### Refined supply held back by mine output constraints Refined supply growth is outpacing that of mines in 2010, due to scrap being diverted from semi fabricators. As a result, refined output is forecast to grow, versus a small decline at the mines. TC/RCs will remain low throughout the outlook period. The miners will remain in a strong position because of the consistently tight concentrate market, which will be due mainly to Chinese smelter expansions. Strong growth in scrap usage by smelters and refineries will underpin a consistently higher growth rate of refined output relative to mine supply. Refined copper production falls less than mine in

CRU International Limited confidential 6 Copper Quarterly October 2010 Executive Preview #### Scrap shortages to continue, supporting refined demand There is no longer a readily available scrap pool for the copper market to draw on. In addition, industrial production remains well below peak levels in the major scrap markets of North America and Western Europe. Therefore, lower quantities of process scrap are being generated by weak industrial activity and the global supply of scrap (using world copper scrap trade as a proxy) remains over 20% below pre-crisis levels. The impact of the tightness is being felt almost entirely in China. In addition, low scrap discounts have seen the smelters outbidding semi fabricators to buy the limited scrap that is available. World scrap imports are slowly recovering, but in H1

#### Deficits to push stocks down to critical levels Exchange stocks have been run down by a third from their peak in February 2010, as consumption growth has outpaced that of supply. This has brought the exchange stock-toconsumption ratio down to the level of a year ago, at the end of the Chinese import boom. Refined production in 2010 and every year through 2013 is expected to be lower than previously forecast. The combination of lower refined output with slowing but still strong consumption growth in 2011 means that the market will move from a slight deficit this year into a larger one of around 375,000t next year. The tight market in 2011 will push stock-toconsumption ratios down to the historic lows last seen in 2004-2005 (0.4-0.5 weeks), where they will remain in 2012, when we expect exchange stocks to fall below 150,000t. Moderating refined consumption growth due to the rationing effect of high prices will shift the market back into surpluses of over 400,000t in both 2013 and 2014. As stocks rise, we expect prices to ease to a cyclical low of $6,900/t ($3.13/lb) in 2014. By 2015, however, the growth in mine supply will lag that of demand and we anticipate that the large surplus will be eroded slightly. Prices will tick up to average $7,200/t ($3

.27/lb) ahead of tighter market conditions in the years ahead. CRU International Limited confidential Copper Quarterly October 2010 Executive Preview 7 Investment money has been an important factor in the recovery in prices, with the GSCI and DJUBS indices alone accounting for investment equivalent to over 600,000t of copper through September 2010. The recovery in market sentiment will only fuel the further rise in allocations to commodities, including copper. The dollar depreciation to over €1.30/$ has also helped push prices back above $8,000/t. However, CRU’s dollar forecasts mean that the currency effect will be a relatively benign influence on prices over the outlook period. Nevertheless, we expect to see investment allocations to continue to support prices in the next couple of years. #### **Points to watch** ### **Upside** - Project financing delays mine project start ups - Oil price spike - Mine underperformance - Chinese new refined intensive semis capacity - Strong demand from highend markets (e.g. strip and sheet in electronics, hybrid and electric vehicles) ### **Uncertainty** ### **Downside** - Financial instability (Euro, non-res. property defaults, derivatives regulation, credit rollovers?) - Macroeconomic risks - Ongoing substitution threats due to high price (Cu/Al price ratio ~ 3.5) - Chinese macroeconomic policy changes - Industry protectionism (antidumping duties, tube) - Scrap availability issues - Non-residential construction - • Currency policies (China, slowdown Japan) - Global semis overcapacity - Environmental policies - More M&As delaying decision making on the production side - • Codelco restructuring © 2010 CRU International Limited confidential
